learningObjective: Distinguish ONNX as an interchange format from any specific runtime (ONNX Runtime, TensorRT importer) that consumes ONNX.
stem: Which statement most accurately describes ONNX's role in the deployment stack?

options.text: ONNX is a high-performance inference runtime that runs models directly on GPU or CPU; converting to another format such as TensorRT is unnecessary because ONNX already ships GPU kernels for every op.
ONNX is a proprietary format used only by Microsoft's ONNX Runtime; other runtimes cannot import it and must convert through TorchScript or SavedModel first.
ONNX is a JIT compiler that lowers PyTorch or TensorFlow models to Triton at load time on the deployment machine; the resulting kernels are cached in the ONNX file for subsequent loads.

ONNX is a serialization format for a graph of standardized operators (with a versioned opset) that different runtimes and compilers can import; performance depends on the runtime that consumes the model, not on ONNX itself.

explanation: ONNX is an open interchange format — a protobuf-encoded graph of standardized operators with an opset version. Multiple runtimes (ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, TVM, IREE, OpenVINO, etc.) can import ONNX and execute it with their own kernels. Performance is a property of the consuming runtime, not of the ONNX file, and 'interchange format ≠ high-performance runtime' is one of the module's canonical boundaries.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: ONNX is a format, not a runtime; ONNX Runtime is a separate project that consumes it.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: ONNX is open and consumed by many runtimes.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: ONNX does not lower to Triton; it is a format, not a JIT compiler.

assumptions: The user is comparing 'the ONNX file' to 'the runtime that loads it'.
nonImplications: Does not imply every op is portable across all runtimes; consumers may not support the full opset.
Does not imply ONNX cannot be compiled AOT; runtimes like TensorRT can build an engine from ONNX at ahead-of-time.
